title: Short-Term Associations Between Relative Humidity and Pediatric Afebrile Seizure Presentations: A Distributed Lag Non-linear Time-Series Study
content: Objective: To evaluate the association between daily meteorological variability and pediatric afebrile seizure presentations using ecological time-series analysis and Distributed Lag Non-linear Models (DLNMs). Methods: This retrospective ecological time-series study was conducted in a tertiary pediatric emergency department in northwestern Türkiye. Seizure-related presentations recorded between January 2019 and December 2023 were screened through a multi-stage clinical validation process. Primary environmental exposure analyses were restricted to the synchronized 2023 dataset. Daily meteorological data were obtained from the regional governmental meteorological monitoring station. Associations between meteorological variables and seizure presentations were assessed using multivariable Quasi-Poisson regression and DLNMs. Results: Among 777 screened seizure-related presentations, 67 children contributing 157 afebrile seizure presentations during 2023 were included. Relative humidity emerged as the strongest independent meteorological predictor of pediatric afebrile seizure presentations. Each 10% increase in relative humidity was associated with an 18.6% increase in seizure incidence (IRR = 1.186; 95% CI: 1.103–1.275; p < 0.001). DLNM analysis demonstrated a significant cumulative delayed effect, with a 10% increase in relative humidity associated with a 15% increase in seizure risk across the subsequent 0–3-day lag period (IRR = 1.15; 95% CI: 1.08–1.22; p < 0.001). Ambient temperature and precipitation demonstrated less consistent associations across analytical approaches, whereas humidity-related effects remained robust throughout all analyses. Conclusions: Higher relative humidity was associated with increased pediatric afebrile seizure presentations and represented the only meteorological exposure demonstrating both significant contemporaneous and cumulative delayed associations. These findings suggest that meteorological variability, particularly relative humidity, may contribute to short-term and delayed fluctuations in seizure-related healthcare utilization among children. Further multicenter prospective studies incorporating individual-level environmental exposure assessment are needed to confirm these findings and clarify the biological mechanisms underlying humidity-associated seizure susceptibility in pediatric populations.
